extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent owners, petitioners, and practitioners involved in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) institution decision evaluating whether to institute inter partes review of specified patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 314, applying standards for claim construction, obviousness, burden of proof, and discretionary denial. The decision reviews the petition, preliminary response, replies, expert declarations, and prior PTAB decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless the information presented in the petition and any response shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates the Petition, Preliminary Response, Reply, Sur-Reply, and the evidence of record to determine whether the evidence presented demonstrates a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail in establishing unpatentability of at least one challenged claim. (Text cites 35 U.S.C. § 314 and describes consideration of the record.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity requirement (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must identify 'with particularity . . . the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. (Cites Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc., and statutory text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in IPRs (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner bears the burden to show that the challenged claims are unpatentable; that burden never shifts to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For institution the threshold is 'reasonable likelihood' under § 314; to prevail at trial petitioner must demonstrate unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (35 U.S.C. § 316(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d)). The decision explains the meaning of 'preponderance' (Concrete Pipe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is less significant than the intrinsic record in determining the legally operative meaning of claim language (citing Phillips, DePuy Spine, C.R. Bard). The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrict claim construction to what is necessary (Nidec)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board provides claim construction only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resolution of an argument does not require construction of a term, the Board may decline to reach a construction at the institution stage (citing Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co.). The decision gives examples where the Board did not construe the preamble or dose-term claim language at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) — applied example
rubrics_metrics.description: A POSITA in this case would have knowledge regarding diagnosis and treatment of angiogenic eye disorders, administration of therapies to treat those disorders, and the ability to understand published results; typically an M.D. or Ph.D. (or equivalent experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board adopted a prior PTAB definition for consistency; the POSITA definition can influence how claim language and prior art disclosures are interpreted at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the whole would have been obvious to a POSITA at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve obviousness using underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness. (Cites Graham v. John Deere.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success (KSR/Dome/Magnum principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an obviousness determination relies on combining references, must show whether a POSITA would be motivated to combine those references and would have a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation/suggestion must be founded in the prior art, not in the applicant’s disclosure (In re Dow; In re Magnum). KSR permits 'obvious to try' reasoning when there is a design need or market pressure and a finite number of identified, predictable solutions; but the combination must still be grounded in the prior art and ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition against hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness reconstruction must take into account only knowledge within the level of ordinary skill at the time and not include knowledge gleaned only from the applicant's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board cites In re McLaughlin to explain that although obviousness judgments are reconstructions, they are proper only if they avoid reliance on applicant-only information; Patent Owner must adduce persuasive evidence of hindsight if alleging it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable weight of claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation (e.g., exclusion criteria) may be entitled to patentable weight and must be considered in the unpatentability analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may dispute whether a limitation is limiting; the Board may assume for institution that a limitation is entitled to patentable weight and then evaluate whether prior art discloses or makes obvious that limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic discretionary-denial factors (when considering denial under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When exercising discretion to deny institution, the Board may consider a set of factors identified in General Plastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seven General Plastic factors (quoted/used by the Board) are: (1) whether the same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims of the same patent; (2) whether at the time of filing of the first petition the petitioner knew of the prior art asserted in the second petition or should have known of it; (3) whether at the time of filing of the second petition the petitioner already received the patent owner’s preliminary response to the first petition or received the Board’s decision on whether to institute review in the first petition; (4) the length of time that elapsed between the time the petitioner learned of the prior art asserted in the second petition and the filing of the second petition; (5) whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent; (6) the finite resources of the Board; and (7) the requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11) to issue a final determination not later than 1 year after the date on which the Director notices institution of review. The Board uses these factors to decide whether to deny institution to prevent serial/abusive petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption/incorporation of prior PTAB decisions for corresponding limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may incorporate and adopt reasoning from prior related PTAB decisions when the claims or limitations are identical or substantially identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Board incorporated reasoning from a prior -00881 Decision to find that many claim limitations were taught by Dixon, then focused only on unresolved differences (the exclusion criteria). The Board may rely on prior findings for portions of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAS Institute principle for institution (all-or-nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board institutes review, it must institute on all challenges presented in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu and related Federal Circuit authority to require a simple yes-or-no institution choice embracing all challenges included in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA applicability / prior art effective-date determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the AIA versions of §§102 and 103 apply based on the effective filing date of the application from which the patent issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application has an effective filing date after March 16, 2013, the AIA versions of 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 apply (explicit citation and example in the decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert declarations and factual testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners often rely on expert declarations to interpret prior art, explain POSITA understanding, and opine on motivation to combine or expected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision relies on the Chaum Declaration (Ex. 1002) as evidence of how a POSITA would interpret prior-art exclusion criteria and whether those criteria would be applied to the challenged claims; expert testimony is weighed in assessing reasonable likelihood of prevailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation vs. obviousness distinction in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art does not literally disclose a limitation, the Board considers whether that limitation is obvious in view of the cited references (as opposed to being anticipated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes that many claim limitations were previously found anticipated by Dixon in a related proceeding, but with an additional exclusion-criteria limitation the Board analyzed whether that limitation was taught or obvious over CATT, MACTEL, and PIER.
